summary: This informational document formally records an existing public key file format used to exchange public keys between different SSH implementations. It also defines a standard text form for SSH public key fingerprints. It was later updated by RFC 9519.

plainLanguage.summary: Different SSH programs saved their public keys in different ways. This writes down one common way to save a key and a standard short nickname, called a fingerprint, for checking it.

subtitle: A plain-text file format for sharing SSH public keys between different SSH programs, plus a standard fingerprint.

tldr.problem: SSH public key authentication needs public keys to be exchanged between client and server, and different SSH implementations needed a common file format to do it.
tldr.mechanism: A key file is a text file wrapped in BEGIN and END marker lines, with optional header lines such as Subject and Comment, followed by the base64-encoded key data. A fingerprint is the MD5 digest of the key data, shown as 16 colon-separated hexadecimal octets.
tldr.outcome: The memo records a format that was already in use and is Informational, not a standard. It was later updated by RFC 9519.

today: RFC 4716 is an Informational memo, not a standard, and it was updated by RFC 9519. It has not been obsoleted.

sections.title: Why a Key File Format Is Needed
sections.content:
The SSH protocol can authenticate with public/private key pairs. Before public key authentication can work, the public keys must first be exchanged between client and server.

RFC 4716 formally describes an existing public key file format that can travel over any of the common file transfer mechanisms. The memo is Informational and states that it does not specify an Internet standard of any kind.

The same keys are also used to authenticate the server, so the RFC adds a way to make a short text string, a fingerprint, that represents a particular public key.
sections.plainLanguage: Before two computers can trust each other, they have to swap keys. This gives everyone the same kind of envelope to put the key in.

sections.title: The Key File Layout
sections.content:
A key file is a text file made of lines. Each line MUST NOT be longer than 72 8-bit bytes, not counting the line ending. Files should be written with the system's local text line ending, and readers SHOULD accept <CR>, <LF> or <CR><LF> in case a file was not transferred as text.

The first line MUST be the literal begin marker ---- BEGIN SSH2 PUBLIC KEY ---- and the last line MUST be the end marker ---- END SSH2 PUBLIC KEY ----.

Between the markers come header lines, then the body. The body is the base64 encoding of the public key data as defined in RFC 4253, Section 6.6: a string naming the certificate or public key format, followed by the key or certificate data. Body lines obey the same 72-byte limit. A line with no colon that is not a continuation line is the first line of the body.
sections.plainLanguage: The key sits between a "start here" line and an "end here" line, like a letter in an envelope, and no line may be longer than a short, fixed length.

sections.title: Header Fields
sections.content:
Headers are RFC 822-style lines of the form Header-tag: Header-value. The tag is case-insensitive, US-ASCII and at most 64 bytes. The value is UTF-8 and at most 1024 bytes. A line ending in a backslash is continued: the backslash and line ending are removed and the next line is appended.

Two headers are defined. Subject holds the login name the key was generated under. Comment holds a user-specified comment that SHOULD be displayed when the key is used, and is suggested to default to user@hostname. Existing practice quotes the comment, and some implementations fail without the quotes. Compliant implementations MUST work when the quotes are omitted, MAY include them, and SHOULD strip matching quotes from the first and last characters.

Tags beginning with x- are reserved for private use. Implementations MUST ignore headers with tags they do not recognise and SHOULD preserve them when editing the file.

The format looks like PEM and OpenPGP armor but is not identical: the delimiters use four dashes and a space instead of five dashes, there is no blank line before the base64, there is no CRC at the end, and header continuation uses a trailing backslash rather than leading whitespace on the next line.
sections.plainLanguage: Above the key you can stick labels like "whose key" and "a note". If a program meets a label it does not know, it just leaves it alone and keeps it.

sections.title: Public Key Fingerprints
sections.content:
SSH security depends on checking public host keys, but keys are long and hard for a person to compare. A fingerprint is a short stand-in for the key.

The fingerprint is the output of the MD5 message digest (RFC 1321) computed over the public key data as specified in RFC 4253, which is the same data that is base64-encoded to form the file body. The 16 output octets are printed as lowercase hexadecimal, separated by colons. The RFC's example is c1:b1:30:29:d7:b8:de:6c:97:77:10:d7:46:41:63:87.
sections.plainLanguage: A key is a very long number, so people check a short nickname made from it instead, a bit like checking the last digits of a long ID number.

sections.title: The Header-Tag Registry
sections.content:
Section 3.3 creates a new namespace of header-tags: case-insensitive US-ASCII strings of at most 64 characters. IANA maintains a registry mapping each tag to the reference that defines it. The initial entries are subject and comment.

Tags starting with x- are private use. All other allocations need IETF consensus.
sections.plainLanguage: There is an official list of label names so two people never use the same label for different things, and a few names are kept free for your own use.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The format has no way to check integrity or detect tampering, so files SHOULD be protected with system measures such as access control lists or UNIX permissions, and SHOULD be moved only over a trusted channel.

Header data is open-ended and can leak information about a user, a key or its use, for example a comment containing a name and address. Sites that deploy the format SHOULD review how headers are used.

The fingerprint uses MD5, which has known collision weaknesses. The RFC argues this use depends only on 2nd-preimage resistance, not collision resistance, and says MD5 is used for historical reasons.
sections.plainLanguage: The file has no lock on it, so keep it somewhere safe, do not put private details in the notes, and remember the nickname trick uses an older method kept for history.

data.title: SSH2 public key file
data.code:
---- BEGIN SSH2 PUBLIC KEY ----
Subject: me
Comment: "1024-bit RSA, created by me@example.com"
AAAAB3NzaC1yc2EAAAABJQAAAIEAiPWx6WM4lhHNedGfBpPJNPpZ7yKu+dnn1SJejgt4
...
---- END SSH2 PUBLIC KEY ----
